correctness.rationale: The Gaussian restriction has argument 2|sin(πx)|/σ, so normalization cancels exp(−2σ⁻²) and gives the stated Bessel ratio. With z=2σ⁻², I₀(2z)/I₀(z)² is asymptotic to √(πz), giving c=√(2π). The ratio minus one is the squared distance to the mean and positive because the factor is nonconstant. Thus σE(σ) has positive finite extrema on the interval after extension at zero. Distinct singleton terms are orthogonal, so the uniform two-sided bound follows. Activating each finite initial segment at small enough positive ρ proves necessity for the supremum over d,ρ, including nonsummable weights; no infinite-dimensional kernel is needed. With t=p/4 the finite sum is exactly Σ_{j≤floor(ρ^{−1/t})} E(ρj^t). The stronger uniform statement E(σ)=c/σ+O(1) on (0,1] gives, after multiplying by ρ, cΣj^{−t}+O(ρ floor(ρ^{−1/t})); this proves the first two limits. For t<1, with A=ρ^{−1/t}, the sum divided by A is a Riemann sum of E(u^t). The portion j/A≤δ has mass at most a constant times δ^{1−t} using the bound by u^{−t}; this justifies the positive finite improper integral and the floor at the upper end. Independence and translation invariance give the exact variance at f=1, where the bias is zero. For general square-integrable input the integrated variance is at most ||f||₂²||K||₂²/M, so the inference about the uniform variance rate is valid. The frozen checker was inspected, not executed: for p=2 it checks a range for scaled energy, not convergence to the stated integral constant. This limitation does not affect the analytic proof.
residual_risks: The asymptotics use a supremum over finite dimensions, not growth at a fixed dimension. The sampling is iid uniform with no observation noise; the conclusion is about this fixed operator.
